text:
My name is Minyeong Yoon, and I am a fourth-year PhD Candidate at the University of Texas at Dallas.
My research examines the effectiveness of crime prevention programs using quantitative methods, including geospatial analysis and causal inference.
Outside of research, I enjoy watching sports, especially baseball ⚾ and hockey 🏒. I’ve recently started learning to play hockey at a local community sports center.

title: Teaching
text: My goal as an educator is to help students move beyond memorizing concepts to critically examining how the criminal justice system operates, whom it affects, and how it might be improved. I view the criminology classroom as a space where students can connect academic knowledge and curiosity with real-world questions about crime, justice, and social responsibility based on evidence. Ultimately, I hope my students can leave my courses better prepared to evaluate information, engage thoughtfully with perspectives different from their own, and contribute to discussions about the criminal justice system.

title: Research
text: My research focuses on evaluating community-based crime prevention and reentry programs, particularly those serving justice-involved youth and emerging adults. I am interested in understanding how program works and individual circumstances shape outcomes such as employment and recidivism, as well as why programs may work differently for different people. Through quantitative research, I seek to identify both the potential and the limitations of these interventions. Ultimately, I hope my research can inform policies and practices that support successful reentry and expand opportunities for justice-involved individuals.

title: Assignment 2
text:
Query Parameters

Search terms: Trump, Harris, and Election
Geography: Worldwide
Time window: Past 5 years
Category: Crime & Justice
Search type: Web Search
Retrieval date and time: September 15, 2026, 1:39 PM

I first collected Google Trends data manually from the website and then reproduced the query using the gtrendsR package in R. The five-year window produced weekly observations. When I changed the time window to the past 30 days, the observations changed to daily intervals.
Google Trends values are normalized relative search-interest scores rather than raw search counts or percentages. A value of 100 represents the peak search interest within the selected query, while 0 indicates very low relative search interest rather than necessarily zero searches.

library(gtrendsR)
library(readr) 

TrumpHarrisElection = gtrends(c("Trump","Harris","election"), onlyInterest = TRUE, gprop = "web", time = "today+5-y", category = 704, ) # last five years
the_df=TrumpHarrisElection$interest_over_time
plot(TrumpHarrisElection)
write_csv(the_df, paste0("gtrends_worldwide_5y_CrimeJustice", Sys.Date(), ".csv")) 



Search Term and Measurement Changes
When I removed Election and repeated the search using only Trump and Harris, the values for the remaining terms remained similar. Because Election had relatively low search interest in the original query, its removal produced only minor changes in the normalized values.

TrumpHarris <- gtrends(c("Trump", "Harris"), onlyInterest = TRUE,  gprop = "web", time = "today+5-y", category = 704, )

TrumpHarris_df <- TrumpHarris$interest_over_time 

I also compared “Kamala Harris” with “Harris.” The two series were different. This matters because a search term does not necessarily measure the exact concept of interest. “Harris” can refer to people, places, or organizations other than Kamala Harris, while “Kamala Harris” is a more specific search term.


Website versus R code
The website and R results were identical when I used the same search terms. The values and overall temporal patterns matched across the two methods.
The two approaches differ methodologically. Manual website downloads require the researcher to record the search settings separately, while R code directly documents many of the query parameters and therefore provides clearer provenance. R is also more scalable because many terms or locations can be collected programmatically rather than downloaded individually. However, R code can be fragile because it relies on the Google Trends service rather than an official public API. Reproducibility is also imperfect because Google Trends relies on sampled and normalized search data.
When I repeated the same R query a few minutes later, the results were slightly different. This suggests that findings based on Google Trends should be interpreted as relative and potentially sample-dependent measures rather than fixed counts.
